name: SeniorDomo
summary: Sells a 4G wristwatch that calls family or a centre when an older person falls.

scene.job: It is a SeniorDomo revolutionizes senior care with advanced telecare services, offering 24/7 protection through GPS, SOS, fall detection, and calls.

title: SeniorDomo
research_summary: SeniorDomo revolutionizes senior care with advanced telecare services, offering 24/7 protection through GPS, SOS, fall detection, and calls.
job: The watch carries its own 4G SIM, so it needs no phone and no wifi. Holding the button for three seconds sends an SOS. If an accelerometer sees a sudden movement or impact, the watch vibrates, beeps, and counts down. The wearer can cancel by holding the button. Otherwise the Family plan calls relatives, and the Professional plan calls Eulen, which can contact 112. Satellites locate it outdoors. Indoors it uses wifi, which can take a minute and fails underground. Pulse is checked about every 10 minutes. The company says the health numbers are not for diagnosis. Battery life is about four days.
who_pays: The watch is 49 euros, down from 99. Family costs 11.99 euros a month on a yearly bill, or 16.99 month to month. The first year on the yearly plan is 192.90 euros including the watch. There is no lock-in and a one-month return. The Professional plan, with Eulen and a MediQuo chat, has no listed price. The company says more than 30 town halls in Spain, France, and Italy also contract it.

traction.text: In August 2019 the Open University of Catalonia said it had been selling for two months around Barcelona, with 12 staff, a watch, room speakers, and a key fob, from 17 to 45 euros a month. On 4 August 2026 the company said 12,500 families use it. That figure is its own.

why_interesting.text: Public telecare in Spain, in its basic form, is a button in the house. This is the outdoor add-on, and the FAQ says families can keep both. Since 2019 the bundle has shrunk from speakers and a social worker to one watch and the Domio app. The countdown exists because the fall sensor false-alarms, and indoor location is approximate.

status.text: Active in October 2026. The shop and an FAQ dated 13 August 2026 were live, and the blog had posts through 29 September 2026. The consent form names the company SeniorDomo, S.L.

title: easierLife
research_summary: easierLife provide older people security in their own homes.
job: easierLife rents alarms for people who want help at the press of a button, at home or outside. A home base, a mobile unit, or a watch can call a professional response centre or the family, and some models add automatic fall detection and GPS. A free app tells relatives when an alarm goes off. The company says the home unit plugs in with no technician, no Wi-Fi, and no home phone, arrives in three to five days, and can be cancelled each month.
who_pays: Private customers pay a monthly fee. The home unit with a response centre is 29.95 euros a month, plus a one-time setup fee of 49.90 euros. With a care grade, the company says the care fund pays 23 euros and easierLife discounts the rest by 6.95 euros, so that home unit costs nothing. The home-and-mobile unit is 44.95 euros a month with a centre, or 19.45 euros after a 25.50 euro care-fund payment. Once a care fund approves the watch, the monthly price falls to 9.45 euros.

why_interesting.text: For a person with a care grade, the basic home alarm can cost nothing after the care-fund payment and the company's own discount, so the insurer is as important a payer as the household. Beside that simple monthly alarm, the register shows repeated public grants for assisted-living research.

name: hip'guard
summary: Sells a belt that inflates airbags at the hips when an older person falls.

scene.job: It is a hip Guard is a company that specializes in the development and production of an airbag belt designed to protect the hips of seniors.

deep_dive.product: Hip Guard is a company that specializes in the development and production of an airbag belt designed to protect the hips of seniors.

title: hip'guard
research_summary: Hip Guard is a company that specializes in the development and production of an airbag belt designed to protect the hips of seniors.
job: Hip'Guard is a belt with two side airbags for older people at risk of a fall. Sensors watch movement, and the company says a side fall is detected in 0.2 seconds and the airbag on that side inflates in 0.08 seconds, before the person hits the ground. The user guide says it is for daily use at home, in a nursing home, or in a rehab centre, and that it is a poor fit for people who move quickly, because a sudden movement can set it off. Helite, a French airbag maker, builds it. After an inflation, the used gas cartridge has to be replaced.
who_pays: The belt is sold online for 755.24 euros including tax, in five sizes. That price covers the belt, a washable cover, two airbags, two gas generators, and the sensor. A price for the replacement gas cartridge was not listed on the shop page.

founders.name: Gérard Thévenot
founders.role: Founder of Helite, the company that makes Hip'Guard

what_it_does.text: Hip'Guard is a belt with two side airbags for older people at risk of a fall. Sensors watch movement, and the company says a side fall is detected in 0.2 seconds and the airbag on that side inflates in 0.08 seconds, before the person hits the ground. The user guide says it is for daily use at home, in a nursing home, or in a rehab centre, and that it is a poor fit for people who move quickly, because a sudden movement can set it off. Helite, a French airbag maker, builds it. After an inflation, the used gas cartridge has to be replaced.

who_pays.text: The belt is sold online for 755.24 euros including tax, in five sizes. That price covers the belt, a washable cover, two airbags, two gas generators, and the sensor. A price for the replacement gas cartridge was not listed on the shop page.

traction.text: The shop page shows no customer reviews. Hip'Guard says the French lab CRITT found that the belt cuts impact force by 90 percent and absorbs nine times more shock than a standard hip pad, and that UGA tested 828 falls and everyday situations, with the belt firing in 9 of 10 side-fall cases and unwanted firing in 1 percent. Those are the company's reports of the tests. Helite says it now has 45 people and distributors in 50 countries. That is the whole airbag business, not a Hip'Guard sales count.

why_interesting.text: A pendant calls for help after a fall. This belt is meant to soften the blow to the hip. The 90 percent impact claim is large, and it is stated on the maker's own certification page rather than in a paper I could read. The user guide also warns that brisk movement can trigger the airbag, so the people who walk most freely may be the worst fit.

status.text: The belt is for sale on hipguard.eu. The legal notice names HELITE SAS, 1 rue de la petite fin, 21121 Fontaine-lès-Dijon, RCS Dijon 883 586 869, with Gérard Thévenot as publication director. Helite dates its own start to 2002 in Dijon.
